analysis.one_liner: Rebuilds the Glass-Steagall wall separating regular banks from securities dealing and insurance.
analysis.headline: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Democrat, a Republican, and an independent cosponsor — but the Senate Banking Committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would restore key parts of the Glass-Steagall Act of 1933, which until the 1990s legally separated ordinary banks (which take deposits and make loans) from investment banks (which underwrite and sell stocks and bonds). It would bar member banks from being affiliated with securities firms, bar securities-firm officers from simultaneously running member banks, and stop banks from selling insurance. Sponsors argued this reduces the risk that risky Wall Street trading inside a regular bank leads to bailouts backed by depositors' money. The bill was introduced in December 2009 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it. [S2] [S3] [S5]
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors and taxpayers, who would no longer have their insured deposits and federal backstop connected to securities underwriting and trading, and to bank-sold insurance. Smaller, separately-chartered banks would also face less competition from giant universal banks that combine all three businesses.

how_it_helps.text: Bars any member bank of the Federal Reserve System from being affiliated, in any manner, with a firm principally engaged in issuing, underwriting, or selling stocks, bonds, and other securities, effective one year after enactment. [S3]

Bars officers, directors, and employees of securities firms from simultaneously serving as officers, directors, or employees of a member bank, with the Federal Reserve able to grant limited exceptions where service would not unduly influence the bank's investment policies. [S2] [S3]
Prohibits depository institutions from engaging in the business of writing or reinsuring insurance, or any insurance-related activity. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Large financial conglomerates — universal banks that combine commercial banking, securities underwriting, and insurance under one roof — would have to separate those businesses within a year, giving up revenue from integrated operations and the implicit subsidy of a bank's deposit base and federal safety net behind securities activities.

drawbacks.text: Opponents argued separation would not have prevented the 2008 crisis, since major failures like Lehman Brothers and Bear Stearns were standalone investment banks outside the banking system — a point supporters of Glass-Steagall's repeal had made. [S3]

The one-year transition and the flat prohibition on any affiliation with a securities firm would have forced the dismantling of existing financial holding companies, disrupting conglomerates whose structures became legal after Glass-Steagall's repeal. [S3]
Banks would no longer be able to offer insurance products to their customers, removing one-stop financial services that many consumers had come to use. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — insulating insured deposits and the federal safety net from securities underwriting and insurance risk — addresses the core conflict that many economists believe made the 2008 bank bailouts possible. The main costs fall on the largest financial firms, not on depositors, though the abrupt one-year timeline and blanket prohibition could have caused real disruption for customers of combined banking-and-insurance services. The strongest honest objection is that standalone securities firms failed in 2008 too, so the wall addresses one channel of contagion rather than all of them.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never scheduled any action on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on December 16, 2009, joined by Republican Senator John McCain and independent Senator Russ Feingold as cosponsors. [S3] [S4]
Six senators cosponsored the bill: one of 40 Senate Republicans, four of 58 Senate Democrats, and the one Senate independent. [S4]
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; the committee took no further action, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large universal banks and financial conglomerates that combine commercial banking, securities underwriting, and insurance are better off — the bill that would have forced them to break apart never advanced, and they kept their combined structure through the Dodd-Frank law enacted later in the same Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan at introduction — a Democratic sponsor plus one Republican, four Democrats, and the chamber's single independent as cosponsors — but no party leadership brought it to a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have forced banks holding insured deposits to separate from securities underwriting and trading within a year. Their interest in keeping the combined model runs against the depositors and taxpayers who bear the risk if securities losses reach the deposit side.

Securities firms would lose the ability to be affiliated with or staff member banks, ending access to the deposit base and bank charter. Separation supporters argue that access lets securities risk ride on the federal banking safety net.

Depository institutions would be barred from writing or reinsuring insurance, taking banks out of insurance sales — a loss for insurers with bank channels and a change for customers who bought insurance through their bank.

Smaller, separately-chartered banks would face less competition from giant firms combining banking, securities, and insurance, and a cleaner separation reduces the chance that the next trading-driven failure drags in the deposit system.
